claims.claim: Rook I links a high-grade uranium resource to the nuclear-fuel bottleneck supporting reliable low-carbon electricity; final construction licensing converts regulatory permission into a construction/execution problem rather than removing it.

Scenario robustness is asymmetric: high-grade low operating-cost potential supports resilience across uranium prices, while the successor bottlenecks are financing, four-year construction, commissioning and the separate operating licence.

factors.name: bottleneckControl
factors.basis: A large high-grade uranium project can add material primary supply if built and licensed to operate.

factors.name: scenarioRobustness
factors.basis: Updated economics remain uranium-price sensitive and pre-production capital rose materially from the original feasibility estimate.

factors.name: supplyChainResilience
factors.basis: Canadian uranium supply diversifies fuel sourcing in a politically stable jurisdiction.

risks.risk: Construction, financing and operating-licence conversion remain necessary before resource quality becomes productive supply.

causalEdges.mechanism: reactor operation requires reliable fuel supply
causalEdges.falsifier: reactor retirements, demand destruction or alternative fuel supply materially eliminate the projected primary-supply need

causalEdges.mechanism: mine/mill construction can convert reserves into production
causalEdges.falsifier: financing, cost, schedule, technical or operating-licence failure prevents economic production

unknowns.unknown: Final construction cost, financing mix and achieved production start remain uncertain.

claims.claim: The key present challenge is capital/schedule conversion: updated pre-production capital increased from roughly C$1.3B to C$2.2B, demonstrating that engineering advancement and inflation can materially reset project economics before production.
Licensing materially de-risks permission but does not prove on-budget construction, financing sufficiency, commissioning or an operating licence.

factors.name: financingRisk
factors.basis: Large remaining construction funding needs can introduce debt, prepayment or equity dilution/partnering tradeoffs.

factors.name: costInflation
factors.basis: Updated capital and operating costs materially exceeded the earlier feasibility basis.

factors.name: confidenceInflation
factors.basis: Regulatory success should not be conflated with completed construction or production.

risks.risk: Further cost escalation or schedule slippage could increase financing needs and dilution/debt burden.
Project economics remain sensitive to uranium prices despite high-grade resource quality.

causalEdges.mechanism: higher capital needs raise financing burden and delay cash generation
causalEdges.falsifier: secured funding plus on-budget milestones materially reduce the remaining capital gap

contradictions.claim: Final construction approval versus unresolved funding/execution burden
contradictions.resolution: No contradiction: permission is a completed milestone while financing and buildout are successor gates.

unknowns.unknown: Ultimate financing mix and resulting dilution/debt economics are not fixed in current evidence.
